endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: This element considers whether performance—including safety-critical behaviors such as escalation and refusal—is consistent across demographic subgroups, and whether it holds across non-standard dialects, accents, colloquialisms, and lower general literacy and health literacy levels.

endorsements.title: A voice-biomarker foundation model for ALS monitoring and Parkinson’s screening
endorsements.quote: Accent, dialect, language, education and recording conditions materially affect acousticfeatures, so models trained on narrow populations can encode and amplify disparities; calibration should be reported at realistic disease prevalence and strati fied by site, device and language.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing machine-assisted translation in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Promote equity and language inclusivity by thoroughly testing all languages used in the health system’s MAT workflow

endorsements.title: Beyond translation: a patient-centered research agenda for artificial intelligence interpreter services in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Without careful eva luation of these novel technologies ’ performance across languages and cultural contexts, they risk increasing communication-based disparities in clinical encounters.

endorsements.title: Governing AI in the Margins: Development of a Human-Centred Governance Framework for Artificial Intelligence in CQC-Regulated Domiciliary Care Using Best-Fit Framework Synthesis
endorsements.quote: Third, an equity gap: AI tools that systematically underperform for carers with non-standard accents or non-English first languages create a two-tier information environment correlated with carer linguistic background, a finding directly supported by the companion empirical data [5].

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence and Medical Translation: An Editorial on the Ethical Considerations for Emerging Technologies in Dermatology
endorsements.quote: Otherwise, targeted efforts will be required to enhance training datasets and methodologies to improve translation accuracy in capturing dermatological terminology and regional linguistic nuances.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence translation in healthcare: an urgent call for evidence-informed policy frameworks
endorsements.quote: Validation processes should therefore incorporate community health workers and cultural mediators from target language communities, not only bilingual evaluators.

endorsements.title: Beyond Time Saved: Implementation, Equity, and the Utility Threshold for Nursing AI Scribes
endorsements.quote: Addressing the ASR equity gap rather than treating it as an afterthought requires conducting subgroup analyses by context-specific axes of linguistic variation, including accent, dialect, and professional characteristics as suggested [ 1 ], and disaggregated reporting on adoption, dropout, and equity metrics of ASR performance.

endorsements.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Integration in Medical Student Education in Somalia and Low-Resource Settings: A Context-Sensitive Implementation Framework
endorsements.issuer: Advances in medical education and practice
endorsements.quote: For educational use, bilingual or trilingual AI outputs should therefore be verified against faculty-approved terminology and, where possible, back-checked between languages before they are incorporated into teaching materials, patient-counseling exercises, or assessment content.

evidence.title: A ‘Silent Trial’ Assessing the Accuracy of Large Language Models for Assisting Community Health Workers in Low-Resource Settings
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on Kinyarwanda spoken CHW-patient encounters
evidence.effect: Encounters recorded in Kinyarwanda were processed by LLMs; o3 performed similarly to CHWs (97.9%) whereas Gemini 2.5-Flash had low accuracy (47.3%).
evidence.quote: Across 150 participating Rwandan CHWs, 429 encounters were recorded (in Kinyarwanda) and then processed by LLMs.

evidence.title: Implementing AI‑Powered Ambient Listening in Medication Reviews: Study Protocol and Pilot Evaluation in Belgian Community Pharmacies
evidence.outcome: Ambient tool performance with regional dialects and accents
evidence.effect: Uneven performance with certain regional dialects and/or accents, leading to incomplete transcripts and summaries; no numbers reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Current challenges include the comprehensive recognition of medication names and uneven performance with certain regional dialects and/or accents, which can lead to incomplete transcripts and summaries.

evidence.title: Accuracy and error patterns of ChatGPT-4o for real-time English–Nepali voice translation: A cross-sectional field evaluation in rural Nepal
evidence.outcome: Translation errors on spontaneous non-English spoken inputs with colloquial, culturally specific speech
evidence.effect: Nepali-to-English mean accuracy 2.23 ± 0.86 vs English-to-Nepali 2.63 ± 0.53; deviations included distortion of meaning (17.1%), omission (14.2%), and addition (11.5%).
evidence.quote: Mean accuracy was higher for English-to-Nepali than Nepali-to-English translation (2.63 ± 0.53 vs 2.23 ± 0.86); 63 of 69 low-accuracy translations (91.3%) occurred in the Nepali-to-English direction.

evidence.title: Between Myths and Metaphors: Rethinking LLMs for SRH in Conservative Contexts
evidence.outcome: LLM interpretation of indirect, colloquial sexual and reproductive health language in clinical interactions
evidence.effect: LLMs struggled with semantic drift, myths, and polysemy when interpreting indirect communication in clinical interactions; no numeric results are reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Our analysis identifies two axes of communication (referential domain and expression approach) and shows LLMs struggle with semantic drift, myths, and polysemy in clinical interactions.
evidence.sample_unit: not reported (clinical observations, interviews, and focus groups with clinicians and patients)

evidence.title: How Good Are Large Language Models at Supporting Frontline Healthcare Workers in Low-Resource Settings – A Benchmarking Study & Dataset
evidence.outcome: LLM response quality when communicating in Kinyarwanda versus English
evidence.effect: Performance degraded slightly in Kinyarwanda, but LLMs remained superior to local clinicians and were over 500 times cheaper per response.
evidence.quote: While performance degraded slightly when LLMs communicated in Kinyarwanda, the LLMs remained superior to clinicians and were over 500 times cheaper per response.

evidence.title: Assessment of the efficacy of ChatGPT responses to bacterial species-specific questions in microbiology
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT answer accuracy across low, moderate, and high language proficiency question formulations
evidence.effect: High-proficiency questions gave a higher share of accurate responses; other proficiency levels yielded mixed/incomplete or inaccurate answers. Overall accurate: 40.4% (3.5) and 56.3% (4.1 mini).
evidence.quote: While high proficiency demonstrated a higher percentage of accurate responses, all other results were either mixed/incomplete, or inaccurate.

evidence.title: AI-Enhanced Speech Recognition in Triage
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Speech-to-text word error rate for High German versus Swiss German dialect, and downstream triage classification accuracy
evidence.effect: WER 2.3% for High German vs 17.66% for Swiss German; classification accuracy still reached 90-100% for ESI levels and CEDIS codes despite the higher WER.
evidence.quote: STT models achieved word error rates (WER) of 2.3% for High German and 17.66% for Swiss German.

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT-4o and Four Open-Source Large Language Models in Generating Diagnoses Based on China's Rare Disease Catalog: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy difference between Chinese and English inputs
evidence.effect: Llama3.1:8b 67.8% English vs 31.4% Chinese (P<.001); Llama3.1:70b 90.1% vs 80.2% (P=.02); qwen2.5 models comparable across languages.
evidence.quote: Language effects varied across models: qwen2.5:7b showed comparable performance in Chinese (51.2%) and English (47.9%; χ²1=0.32, P=.57), whereas Llama3.1:8b exhibited significantly higher English accuracy (67.8% vs 31.4%; χ²1=40.20, P<.001).

evidence.title: AI-TransLATE: Validation of a Speech-Based Multilingual Interpretation Tool in Critical Care
evidence.outcome: Interpretation quality across four languages using scripted ICU scenarios
evidence.effect: Composite scores were acceptable (≥16/20) across all languages. Spanish and Turkish performed consistently well; Chinese and Arabic showed variability due to omissions and terminology errors.
evidence.quote: Spanish and Turkish performed consistently well; Chinese and Arabic showed variability due to omissions and terminology errors.

evidence.title: Accent related errors in clinical speech transcription and a LLM-based remedy
evidence.outcome: ASR transcription error (WER) for native vs non-native English accented speech
evidence.effect: Non-native speakers had higher WER across all models; Whisper disparity β = 11.0 (95% CI 1.0–21.0, p = 0.031); WhisperX β = 3.4 (p = 0.07).
evidence.quote: The greatest disparity was observed in Whisper ( β = 11.0, 95% CI [1.0, 21.0], p = 0.031), while WhisperX showed a smaller, marginally significant difference ( β = 3.4, p = 0.07).

evidence.title: Integrating Large Language Models Into Trauma Education for Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Pilot Trial
evidence.outcome: Effect of non-English prompting on LLM performance
evidence.effect: Non-English prompting likely contributed to lower AI performance; students reported vague or overly general responses.
evidence.quote: The use of non-English prompting likely contributed to lower AI performance, underscoring the importance of language alignment in LLM applications.
languages: non-English (prompting language not specified in abstract)

evidence.title: AI-generated clinical summaries: errors and susceptibility to speech and speaker variability
evidence.outcome: Scribe accuracy across accents, personality styles, and speech impairments
evidence.effect: No significant differences across personality types (all p>0.05) or accents (patients p=0.851; doctors p=0.980); phonological impairment markedly reduced word recognition (p<0.001), while cleft palate and vowel disorders were near-perfect.
evidence.quote: Conversely, speech impairments differed: cleft palate and vowel disorders were near-perfect, whereas phonological impairment markedly reduced recognition (p<0.001).
languages: English (international accents: Chinese, Indian and others)

evidence.title: Error Detection and Correction in Chinese Radiology Reports Using Large Language Models: Real-World Clinical Validation Study
evidence.outcome: LLM error detection performance across Chinese and English reports
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-R1 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet detected 94% and 93% of errors in external English MIMIC-III reports; internal Chinese validation 83% and 80%.
evidence.quote: On the external validation set, DeepSeek-R1 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet achieved detection rates of 94% (95% CI 89%-97%) and 93% (95% CI 88%-97%), respectively.

evidence.title: Patient-Facing AI Chatbot Treatment-Direction Advice in Orthodontic Health Communication: A Scenario-Based Comparison with Expert Consensus
evidence.outcome: Chatbot performance on Turkish-language patient-oriented scenarios
evidence.effect: Performance in Turkish varied widely across chatbots (37.5% to 82.5% concordance); single-language design limits conclusions on non-English performance.
evidence.quote: Under the tested single-date, single-language, and single-run conditions, the findings represent a conditional snapshot rather than a time-invariant ranking of model capability.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot first responses (40 scenarios x 4 chatbots)

evidence.title: Out of the Box, into the Clinic? Evaluating State-of-the-Art ASR for Clinical Applications for Older Adults
evidence.outcome: ASR word error rate on older Dutch adults' speech, generic versus fine-tuned models
evidence.effect: Generic multilingual models outperformed models fine-tuned for older Dutch adults' speech, so they generalise well out of the box. Some inputs still caused a high word error rate.
evidence.quote: Our results show that generic multilingual models outperform fine-tuned models, which suggests recent ASR models can generalise well out of the box to real-world datasets.

evidence.title: Script Gap: Evaluating LLM Triage on Indian Languages in Native vs Romanized Scripts in a Real World Setting
evidence.outcome: LLM triage performance on romanized versus native-script health queries
evidence.effect: Consistent degradation for romanized messages, with gaps reaching up to 24 points across languages and models; nearly 2 million excess triage errors estimated at the partner organization.
evidence.quote: Our results reveal consistent degradation in performance for romanized messages, with gap reaching up to 24 points across languages and models.
languages: Indian languages (five, not named in abstract)

evidence.title: When Vocabulary Comprehension Fails Clinical Reasoning: Evaluating Therapy Bots' Safety Risks for Generation Alpha
evidence.outcome: Model performance on non-standard youth slang, colloquialisms, and informal style
evidence.effect: Vocabulary-comprehension gap of 10-14pp, widening with ambiguity (7pp to 18pp); informal style bias 24pp.
evidence.quote: The gap is architecturally consistent and widens with ambiguity (7pp -> 18pp).

evidence.title: Accents Still Confuse AI: Systematic Errors in Speech Transcription and LLM-Based Remedies
evidence.outcome: Transcription accuracy of Whisper and WhisperX across native and non-native English accents
evidence.effect: Both models had significantly higher errors for non-native speakers.
evidence.quote: We measured transcription accuracy of Whisper and WhisperX on clinical texts across native and non-native English speakers and found that both models have significantly higher errors for non-native speakers.

evidence.title: Encoding Fidelity and Coherent Misalignment in Non-English Clinical AI
evidence.outcome: Semantic encoding fidelity and output degradation for non-English Indian languages in clinical text
evidence.effect: EFI degrades by ~90% for all non-English Indian languages tested (p < 10^-13); Kannada shows 1.72-2.05x variance amplification; code-switching and orthographic corruption of medical terms seen in Mistral.
evidence.quote: Large Language Models show significant systematic degradation of this assumption for non-English languages, producing outputs that are internally consistent but semantically degraded.
evidence.sample_unit: medical sentences and scenarios across languages

evidence.title: Technical Synthesis and Deployment Framework for a Pashto-Centric Pharmaceutical Information System Utilizing Gemma-4 Multimodal Architectures and Local Knowledge Bases
evidence.outcome: Retrieval performance on Pashto inflected terms, transliterated drug names, and dialect variants versus English keyword baseline
evidence.effect: Baseline English keyword search returned zero results for Pashto input; the morphology-aware MARS retrieval achieved substantial recall (no exact figures in abstract).
evidence.quote: Evaluation on a benchmark of 50 Pashto medical queries across three categories (inflected terms, transliterated drug names, dialect variants) shows that MARS achieves substantial retrieval recall where the baseline English keyword search returns zero results for Pashto input.

evidence.title: The Potential Clinical Utility of the Customized Large Language Model in Gastroenterology: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Customized LLM accuracy on Korean-language questions with Korean versus English medical terminology
evidence.effect: Customized LLM answered 8/15 correctly with Korean terms; replacing Korean terms with English improved performance by two additional knowledge-based questions, matching the fellow's score.
evidence.quote: When the standardized Korean medical terms were replaced with English terminology, the LLM's performance improved, answering two additional knowledge-based questions correctly, matching the fellow's score.

evidence.title: Dictionary-Augmented Large Language Model Postprocessing for Bilingual Code-Switched Medical Speech Recognition: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: code-switched term normalization need
evidence.effect: 16,754/23,652 sentences (70.83%) contained at least one term requiring normalization.
evidence.quote: Of the 23,652 sentences, 6898 (29.17%) required no dictionary-based modifications, indicating that 16,754 (70.83%) contained at least one term requiring normalization.

commentary.bottom_line: No study tests whether evaluating AI on non-standard dialects, accents, colloquialisms, or low-literacy inputs improves accuracy or safety once a tool is deployed. Twenty-two hazard studies, most of them simulations or benchmarks, report performance gaps for these inputs in many settings, while several report small or no gaps.

perspectives.view: No included study compares deployments with and without this kind of subgroup testing. The 22 hazard studies are mostly level 4 and 5 simulations and benchmarks with inconsistent results. One UK scribe study found no accent differences, and one Indian benchmark found gaps of up to 24 points. These studies show the problem exists but not that testing fixes it.

Triage accuracy fell by up to 24 points for romanized queries, with an estimated nearly 2 million excess triage errors at one organization. Nepali-to-English translation distorted meaning in 17.1% of utterances. Swiss German raised word error rate to 17.66%, yet triage accuracy stayed at 90-100%. This suggests testing may need to measure downstream clinical outputs as well as transcription error.

Results differed by model even within the same language. On Kinyarwanda encounters, o3 reached 97.9% accuracy and Gemini 2.5-Flash reached 47.3%. The 8-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model scored 67.8% in English and 31.4% in Chinese, while qwen2.5 models scored similarly in both. These results suggest that a test of one model or version may not carry over to another.

Whisper showed a word error rate disparity of 11.0 for non-native English speakers. ChatGPT gave more accurate answers to questions phrased at high language proficiency, which may serve as a proxy for literacy. A youth slang benchmark found a 10-14 point comprehension gap. None of these studies enrolled low-health-literacy patients directly.

A regulatory discussion paper lists consistency across dialects, accents, colloquialisms, and literacy levels as an element to consider, including escalation and refusal behavior. It is a discussion paper and does not set a binding requirement. None of the supplied studies measures compliance with it or its effect.

In Kinyarwanda, LLM responses degraded slightly but cost over 500 times less per response than local clinicians. In Korean nursing notes, 70.83% of sentences contained code-switched terms that required normalization. Building test sets may therefore require locally sourced language samples. No study reports the staff time or cost of doing this testing.

Phonological speech impairment markedly reduced scribe word recognition. An English keyword search returned zero results for Pashto queries. Patients whose speech or language falls outside the training data may receive incomplete or empty outputs without knowing it. One commentary recommends that community health workers and cultural mediators take part in validation.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI deployments that did and did not receive pre-deployment testing on dialect, accent, colloquial, and low-literacy inputs. They should measure whether testing detected failures, whether it changed model selection or configuration, and whether patient-level errors fell afterward. They should also report the cost and staffing needed to build and maintain local test sets.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Several hazard studies involved limited English proficiency, rural, or low-income groups, mostly in Rwanda, Nepal, India, and Pakistan. Only one examined low-proficiency phrasing, and it did not enroll patients. The evidence therefore does not show whether testing protects US Medicaid, safety-net, or low-health-literacy patients.
